newsitem.title: USA: States reach agreements with Prudential on insurance sales. [CORRECTED 23:58 GMT]
newsitem.headline: States reach agreements with Prudential on insurance sales. [CORRECTED 23:58 GMT]

text.p: Florida, Texas and Massachusetts reached separate multi-million dollar agreements Thursday with Prudential Insurance Co. of America, settling allegations the insurer used deceptive tactics to sell life insurance.

In December, Florida, along with Texas, Massachusetts and California, urged a federal judge to reject a class-action settlement by Prudential, calling it unfair to consumers. Under that settlement, reached in September, Prudential agreed to pay at least $410 million to as many as 10.7 million policyholders who bought permanent life insurance policies between 1982 and 1995. (Corrects from "between 1982 and 1985.")
The proposed class action settlement could cost Prudential as much as $1.2 billion in direct expenses and could have a total value to policyholders of almost $2 billion.
A hearing to determine the fairness of the proposed settlement is scheduled to begin Monday in U.S. district court in Newark, N.J.

Florida has been one of the most outspoken critics of Prudential's proposed class-action settlement of consumer sales complaints. But state officials said in Tallahassee that Florida would now drop its opposition.

Under Florida's settlement, Prudential agreed to pay $15 million to the state and make restitution to an estimated 128,000 Floridian policyholders to settle state charges it cheated life-insurance customers.
A lawyer for the Florida Department of Insurance estimated that the average excess premium paid by affected customers was $2,300, but some customers had overpaid by as much as $7,000.

Florida State Treasurer and Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson said the Florida settlement will benefit policyholders across the United State, not in only Florida, because Prudential has agreed to amend its class action settlement.
"This is an amendment to the entire class-action settlement process, so it will help those across the country benefit from the changed class-action proposed settlement," Nelson said.
In early December, Nelson charged Prudential with obstructing a state probe into allegations that the company misrepresented its insurance policies as investments.
The commissioner at that time threatened that if the company did not provide requested documents, it could face sanctions, possibly including the loss of its license to operate in Florida.
Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth also had been investigating the company to ensure that policyholders were fairly compensated.
In a separate settlement Thursday, the Texas Department of Insurance also reached an agreement with Prudential, but additional details were not immediately available.
Prudential agreed late last week to pay $384,200 to settle a lawsuit brought by Virginia. It acknowledged that some policyholders may have been misled by Prudential agents.
Florida has been one of the staunchest critics of the settlement.
Information on the Massachusetts settlement, which was confirmed by that state's Department of Insurance, was not immediately available.
California said it still opposed Prudential's settlements and declined to comment on whether it was in talks with the company about a possible agreement.
